turns.content: Alright draft is up. Headline is "Root Cause: Nitrogen-Induced Taproot Suppression." Four edge tubes show 40% loss. Storm data is still in the slide. Need that cut. Weather is excluded under the contract so it can't be on the causal line.

Before I help cut anything, one flag: the contract excluding weather governs what's *covered*, not what *caused* the loss. Those are two different lines. If the storm data gets removed from the causal analysis because of a coverage clause, the "Root Cause" headline stops being a finding and becomes a conclusion shaped around the contract. If anyone downstream (adjuster, opposing expert, court) sees the underlying tube data, that's the exact hole they'll drive through.

And the pattern itself is nagging me. Four *edge* tubes at 40% loss is a spatial signature. Nitrogen-induced taproot suppression from a uniform application would typically show up across the field, not concentrated at the perimeter. Edge concentration is what you'd expect from wind exposure, water movement, or mechanical damage during a storm. So the storm data isn't just sitting awkwardly in the slide, it may be explaining the distribution better than the headline does.

What I'd suggest instead of a straight cut:

- **Keep the storm data, but move it.** Put it in a "factors considered" section, either ruled out with a stated reason (timing doesn't match, interior tubes show the same loss, soil moisture data contradicts it) or acknowledged as a contributing factor that's separated from the covered mechanism.
- **Soften the headline if the rule-out isn't airtight.** "Primary Mechanism: Nitrogen-Induced Taproot Suppression" or "Findings" carries the same weight without claiming exclusivity you may not be able to defend.
- **Address the edge pattern directly.** If there's a nitrogen-based reason the loss is edge-concentrated (overlap on applicator passes, headland double-application), say it. That would actually strengthen the case a lot.

If you paste the slide text or upload the deck, I can restructure it along those lines and tighten the causal section. If you've got interior tube data that shows comparable loss, that's the thing that legitimately sidelines the storm, and I'd lead with it.

Two things you'll want to be aware of before this goes out, because they'll come up:

1. **The interior gap cuts both ways.** "Unmonitored, can't compare" means you can't rule the storm *in*, but it also means you can't rule it *out*. 2. **"Root Cause" is still doing a lot of work.** With only edge tubes and no interior baseline, the honest strength of the finding is "consistent with," which is what the Findings bullet says. The headline asserts more than that. If you want a headline that can't be turned against you, "Primary Finding: Nitrogen-Induced Taproot Suppression" says the same thing without claiming you've excluded everything else.
